broccoli-and-cauliflower-cooked-fat-adde.title: Broccoli and cauliflower, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Broccoli and cauliflower are two members of the cruciferous vegetable family, often prepared together. When cooked with added fat (oil, butter) they retain a crisp texture and develop a richer flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Broccoli and cauliflower belong to the Brassicaceae family.
Both vegetables are rich in glucosinolates, compounds that may support the body’s detox pathways.
Heat cooking reduces some vitamin C, but many phytochemicals remain intact.
Traditional cooking methods use steaming, but adding fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble nutrients.
They appear in soups, stews, casseroles, and as side dishes in cuisines worldwide.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Rich in phytochemicals
items.content: Sulforaphane and indole‑3‑carbinol have antioxidant and anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Adding fat increases the bioavailability of vitamins A, D, E, and K.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to broccoli or cauliflower.

items.title: Excessive fat intake
items.content: Using too much oil or butter can make the dish high in calories.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Cruciferous vegetables can cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Prolonged high heat destroys some vitamin C and folate.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté, stir‑fry, or roast broccoli and cauliflower with a modest amount of oil or butter. Season with herbs, garlic, or a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor. Serve as a side, in vegetable medleys, or incorporated into stews and casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh florets in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or container for up to 5 days. Cooked vegetables should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and consumed within 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked celery consists of the stalks of Apium graveolens that have been peeled and boiled until tender. Cooking softens the characteristic crisp texture while retaining its distinctive aroma and adding a mild sweetness. It is used in soups, stews, salads, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Celery belongs to the Apiaceae family, the same as carrots and parsley.
It is very low in calories – about 16 kcal per 100 g of cooked product.
Ancient Romans used celery as a flavoring herb in many dishes.
While most people think of the stalks, celery roots are also edible.
Stalk color can range from light‑green to darker shades depending on the variety.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Celery provides flavonoids and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Its dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements and overall gut health.

items.title: May lower blood pressure
items.content: Naturally occurring nitrates can help relax blood vessels.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Celery supplies potassium, magnesium and phosphorus, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Practically fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to celery, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Celery contains oxalates, which in high amounts can contribute to kidney stone formation.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: When buying non‑organic celery, it is advisable to wash thoroughly and, if possible, peel before cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve cooked celery as a side dish with meat, fish or poultry, add it to vegetable stews, soups and purees. It can be diced for salads with yogurt dressing or used in cold appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked celery in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

macaroni-or-noodles-with-cheese-canned.title: Macaroni or noodles with cheese, canned

content.title: About
content.content: Canned macaroni with cheese is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of short pasta coated in a creamy cheese sauce and sealed in an airtight can. It is designed for quick preparation: simply open the can and heat the contents.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial macaroni‑and‑cheese product appeared in the United States in the 1930s.
Canning allows the product to be stored for 2‑3 years without added preservatives.
The sauce often contains a dry cheese powder that reconstitutes when heated.
Canned macaroni and cheese is a staple of military rations and backpacking meals.
In Russia, such products are popular in regions with limited fresh‑food access.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The pasta provides a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: The cheese sauce adds both dairy and plant‑based protein, supporting tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cheese component is enriched with calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product supplies thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Convenience and speed
items.content: Fast preparation helps maintain a regular eating schedule when time is limited.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Canned meals often contain elevated salt levels, which may be unsuitable for hypertension.

items.title: Lactose and dairy protein
items.content: The product is not suitable for people with lactose intolerance or dairy allergies.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The creamy sauce increases the caloric load, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Some versions may contain stabilizers and flavor enhancers that can cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open the can, pour the contents into a saucepan or microwave‑safe bowl and heat for 3‑5 minutes, stirring occasionally. For extra flavor you can add fresh vegetables, herbs, or a dash of hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, consume within 2‑3 days and keep refrigerated in an airtight container.

oatmeal-instant-maple-flavored-fat-added.title: Instant Oatmeal, Maple Flavor, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: Instant oatmeal with maple flavor and added fat is a ready‑to‑eat breakfast that dissolves quickly in hot water or milk. The added fat enhances taste and creates a creamier texture, while maple syrup provides sweetness and a distinctive aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Instant oatmeal was first developed in the early 20th century for soldiers and travelers needing quick nutrition.
Maple flavor is derived from natural maple syrup or natural flavorings.
Adding fat raises the product’s energy density and promotes a feeling of fullness.
Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown for over 10,000 years.
Oat flakes can be made from whole grains, hull‑less oats, or a blend of both.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oatmeal contains soluble beta‑glucan fiber, which helps regulate blood sugar and lower cholesterol.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy release, keeping you full for several hours.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Added plant oils (e.g., sunflower or rapeseed) supply essential fatty acids.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats are a good source of thiamine, niacin, and folate, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The product provides magnesium, iron, and zinc, important for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Oat allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to oats or added ingredients.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The added fat increases calories, so portion size should be monitored in weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Maple flavor often comes with added sugar, which may be unsuitable for individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Oats are frequently processed on equipment shared with wheat, posing a risk of gluten contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour 200 ml of hot water or milk over the oatmeal, stir, and let it sit for 1–2 minutes. You can enhance it with nuts, berries, honey, or yogurt for extra flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. After opening, use within 4–6 weeks. Discard if you notice moldy odor or off‑flavors.
